newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil won't bend on 'social clause' at WTO summit.
newsitem.headline: Brazil won't bend on 'social clause' at WTO summit.

text.p: Brazil, Latin America's largest country, will not bend to demands for trade-linked labor standards, the country's Foreign Minister said on Monday.

Luiz Felipe Lampreia, summing up Brazil's position ahead of next week's first ministerial encounter of the World Trade Organization, said Brazil was in the clear majority in its opposition to the so-called "social clause".
"Brazil's position is shared by the vast majority and is opposed only by a few countries, principally the United States and France," Lampreia said.

"The Brazilian government is...strongly opposed, like most countries, to the protectionist use of workers rights, or whatever discrimination against a country with lower wages or less developed living standards than others."

Brazil, like many developing nations, fears an attempt by countries like the United States at the WTO summit in Singapore to reduce its comparative wage advantage by tying a minimum set of workers rights to trade issues.

The issue of the "social clause" is one of a host of disagreements that threatens to turn the December 9-13 meeting into a shouting match rather than the trouble-free encounter its organizers have been working feverishly to achieve.
"Singapore will not be just a formal meeting, but a meeting for negotiations," Lampreia said.
The foreign minister did not comment in detail on other positions Brazil would take in Singapore.
But he reiterated Brasilia's concern at pressure for faster liberalization, not just within the framework of the WTO but also with regard to the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).
The creation of the FTAA, a hemispheric free trade zone due to come into being by 2005, has evolved into a low-key tussle between Washington and Brasilia.

Trade analysts say Brasilia is keen to ensure the Mercosur customs union, grouping Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay in addition to Brazil, is sufficiently consolidated to stand up against Washington's NAFTA (North America Free Trade Agreement) before giant steps are taken towards the FTAA.
"We have carried out unilaterally a huge economic opening," Lampreia said, citing a decline in average Brazilian import tariffs to 12.5 percent now from 58 percent in 1989.

"But the government could not be so careless as to submit our national industry to another (trade) shock," he said, referring to some calls for even speedier progress on tariff reductions. "This would mean the liquidation of a large part of Brazilian industry."
Nevertheless, Lampreia played down the significance of discord, pointing out that "in international trade, there are no angels".
He noted that every country had its own agenda based on domestic considerations and that "the nature of the game" was to haggle for the best bargain each could get.
